## The puzzle

Within 48 hours of the 28 February 2026 strikes, an unusual pattern surfaced. The two Sunni Gulf monarchies with the deepest US security relationships — Saudi Arabia and the UAE — were *privately* and *publicly* pushing Trump to continue the war until Iran's regime collapsed. Yet both of them, plus Qatar, Kuwait, and Bahrain, declined repeated US asks for military support to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi denied use of Prince Sultan Airbase. Qatar's Emir lobbied Washington against using Gulf bases within 48 hours of war initiation. Kuwait sat on its hands.

So they wanted the war won. They would not pay to win it. Why?

::: {.bottom-line}
**Bottom line.** The single mechanism that resolves the paradox is *forward-looking risk minimization under uncertainty about whether Iran survives the war.* A "weakened but not destroyed" Iran will retaliate against accessible Gulf targets, so the Gulf wants Iran finished. But visible alignment raises future target priority for an Iran that *does* survive — so MBS pushes privately and lets UAE be the public voice. Both halves of the paradox come from the same calculus. Four secondary mechanisms (omnibalancing, the [2023 China-brokered détente]{.gloss data-gloss="saudi-iran-2023-rapprochement"}, [Vision 2030]{.gloss data-gloss="vision-2030"} economic exposure, the [Yemen lesson]{.gloss data-gloss="yemen-lesson"}) explain *which* Gulf state is more or less constrained — not *why* the underlying pattern exists.
:::

[For Q12.4 the textbook frame — Olson-Zeckhauser free-riding — turns out to be wrong, and the right frame (Lake's hierarchy / Posen's patron-client) is not in the canonical IR syllabus. The DA-corrected mechanism set then collapses to a single load-bearing one when the Iran_war briefing was reviewed. Both moves are described below.]{.column-margin .detail-only}

::: {.detail-only}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Methodology — the eight-step protocol used here {.detail-only}

This chapter applies the project's standard protocol: (1) pre-write a prior; (2) corpus passage extraction; (3) think-tank cross-check; (4) opposing steel-mans; (5) pre-DA synthesis; (6) hostile devil's advocate; (7) reconcile; (8) source-confidence tier audit + Bayesian framing + pre-mortem. After protocol completion, an **external corpus review** against an independently-prepared question briefing surfaced an empirical-premise correction (the canonical "March 16 Trump-GCC bilateral call" was not a bilateral diplomatic ask; it was Trump's March 14–16 Truth Social broadcasts to international consumers) and a stronger single-mechanism account that strictly improved on the multi-mechanism reconciliation. The corrected synthesis is below.
:::

:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage1"}
**Three opening hypotheses.** The puzzle admits at least three readings. The textbook one — [*free-riding*]{.gloss data-gloss="olson-zeckhauser"} — predicts that small allies of a security-providing hegemon systematically under-contribute. The second reads the Gulf as *constrained* by domestic politics: Sunni monarchies with restive Shia populations cannot openly fight a Sunni-Shia regional war without inviting unrest. The third reads the Gulf as *responding to Iran's strategy*: Iran attacked every GCC capital regardless of whether they contributed, which fits coercive escalation rather than retaliation deterrence.
:::

::: {#cr-stage2}
```{mermaid}

  E1[Iran attacked<br/>ALL GCC capitals]
  E2[Saudi denied<br/>airspace pre-war,<br/>not as bargaining]
  E3[GCC-US is asymmetric<br/>clientelist, not<br/>alliance of equals]

  F -->|fails on| E2
  F -->|wrong frame| E3
```

:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage2"}
**The free-rider reading breaks on three pieces of evidence.** Iran's strategy was not retaliation against contributors; it was offensive coercive escalation [Schelling's "[threat that leaves something to chance]{.gloss data-gloss="schelling-something-to-chance"}," applied as a gambit to break GCC collective-action capacity]{.detail-only}. Saudi airspace denial pre-dated the war (Fox News, 30 January 2026) — it was not a wartime bargain over costs; it was a structural position. And the underlying relationship is not an alliance of equals (the model Olson-Zeckhauser was built on); it is a [hierarchical clientelist relationship]{.gloss data-gloss="lake-hierarchy"} in which the small client can constrain the large patron's action when patron requests damage client interests.
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage3"}
**The DA-corrected synthesis: four mechanisms.** Replacing Olson-Zeckhauser with Lake's hierarchy and adding [omnibalancing]{.gloss data-gloss="omnibalancing"} produced a four-mechanism reconciliation — domestic-Shia threat, the 2023 China-brokered Saudi-Iran détente, Vision 2030 economic exposure, and the Yemen lesson — each operative for a different sub-set of Gulf states. This was a substantial improvement. It explained *which* Gulf state was more or less constrained. It did not yet explain *why* the underlying behavior pattern existed in the first place.
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage4"}
**The single-mechanism account.** A briefing-review pass surfaced a stronger reading: Hussein Ibish's *post-war retaliation risk* mechanism explains both halves of the paradox from one forward-looking calculus. A weakened-but-surviving Iran will retaliate against accessible Gulf targets, so the Gulf wants Iran finished — *push for regime change.* Visible alignment raises future target priority if Iran does survive — so *decline to be visibly the platform.* The four DA-derived mechanisms are now *modifiers* explaining cross-state variation, not independent primary mechanisms. This is strictly better than the four-mechanism reconciliation: same predictive power for cross-state variation, plus a coherent account of why the puzzle exists.
:::

:::

**Reading the chart.** Each row is one mechanism. The light grey bar shows posterior P(operative) — how likely the mechanism is at play. The colored foreground bar shows posterior P(load-bearing) — how much of the puzzle the mechanism actually explains. Color encodes the [tier badge]{.gloss data-gloss="source-confidence-tier"}: green = T1 (multi-source verified), yellow = T2 (single-source named), red = T3 (inference from evidence), grey = T4 (conjecture). The dashed blue line at 0.5 marks the load-bearing threshold; above the line means the mechanism is doing more than chance work in the synthesis. The headline finding — **M0 at 65% P(load-bearing)** — is *not* T1, because Ibish's specific framing has not yet been independently corroborated in the wider think-tank literature. Treat it as the best current single-mechanism account, not as established.

### Figure 2 — Per-state typology

| State | Type | Dominant mechanisms |
|---|---|---|
| **Saudi Arabia** | Hawkish-hedger | M0 + M2 (détente) + M3 (Vision 2030) + M4 (Yemen) + M6 (clientelist); denied airspace as clientelist signal |
| **UAE** | Most-hawkish-most-targeted | M0 + M3 (FDI/economy) + M5 (responding to Iran's gambit) + M7 (bilateral divergence from Saudi) |
| **Qatar** | Mediator under fire | M0 + M5 (Iran gambit; lost LNG capacity) + [biased-mediator role (Kydd)]{.gloss data-gloss="kydd-biased-mediator"} |
| **Bahrain** | Sectarian-constrained | M1 (omnibalancing — load-bearing) + M6 (clientelist); domestic Shia constraint dominant |
| **Kuwait** | Parliamentary-exposed | M1 (smaller Shia population, but parliament) + M7 (consensus tradition) |
| **Oman** | Pure mediator | Kydd biased-mediator (T1) — different from Sub-I/II entirely |
| **Iraq** | Shia battleground | Iran-aligned militias active; out of Q12.4 scope |

[The critical empirical fact differentiating UAE/Saudi from Bahrain/Kuwait/Qatar: **pipeline bypass capacity**. Petroline ~7 mb/d (Saudi), Habshan-Fujairah ~1.5 mb/d (UAE) — nothing for the others. Bypass gives Saudi/UAE more freedom of action. They used it differently (UAE more hawkish-public, Saudi more hedging). Bypass capacity is necessary but not sufficient — supporting M7 (intra-court politics) over a pure structural reading.]{.column-margin}

### Figure 3 — Why the textbook frame fails

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph OZ [Olson-Zeckhauser 1966]
    direction LR
    A1[Alliance of<br/>formal equals]
    A1 --> A2[Public good:<br/>shared security]
    A2 --> A3[Predict:<br/>small allies<br/>under-contribute]
  end
  subgraph LK [Lake 2009 hierarchy]
    direction LR
    B1[Asymmetric<br/>clientelist relationship]
    B1 --> B2[Patron provides<br/>security; client<br/>cedes some sovereignty]
    B2 --> B3[Predict:<br/>client constrains<br/>patron action when<br/>patron requests damage<br/>client interests]
  end
  E[Saudi airspace denial<br/>predates war] -.->|fails| A3
  E -.->|fits| B3
  classDef oz fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#d4a72c
  classDef lk fill:#dafbe1,stroke:#2da44e
  classDef ev fill:#ffe5d9,stroke:#cf222e
  class A1,A2,A3 oz
  class B1,B2,B3 lk
  class E ev
```

Olson-Zeckhauser was designed for alliances of formal equals (NATO). The Gulf-US relationship is an asymmetric clientelist relationship — a different game-theoretic object with different equilibria. Saudi airspace denial is not under-contribution within an intact alliance; it is a clientelist signal that the patron has violated implicit norms (no consultation; demanding action without burden-sharing on cost).

::: {.detail-only}

### Figure 4 — Source-confidence tier breakdown {.detail-only}

Of the synthesis's load-bearing claims:

- **[T1]{.tier .tier-1} multi-source verified:** Iran attacked all GCC capitals; Bahrain 350+ detentions in war period; QatarEnergy LNG force majeure (March 24); 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement was China-brokered; Petroline / Habshan-Fujairah capacities; Saudi airspace position predates the war.
- **[T2]{.tier .tier-2} single-source named:** UAE OPEC+ exit; Saudi-UAE coordination fractures; Iran chose Oman for mediation; Trump's "biggest surprise" framing; Vision 2030 / NEOM constraint on Saudi hawkishness.
- **[T3]{.tier .tier-3} inference from evidence:** Iran's strategy as offensive coercive gambit (rather than retaliation deterrent); domestic-Shia-population threat as binding constraint on Sunni monarchies; GCC bureaucratic incoherence reflects intelligence-vs-foreign-ministry gap.
- **[T4]{.tier .tier-4} conjecture:** none in the load-bearing path post-revision.

The biggest inferential claim ([T3]{.tier .tier-3}) is the reframing of Iran's strategy as offensive gambit rather than deterrent. This is a methodological choice (reading the same evidence through different framework) rather than a factual claim. The omnibalancing/domestic-Shia-threat claim ([T3]{.tier .tier-3}) does substantial analytical work and is flagged for further verification with primary MENA-studies sources.

:::

## Pre-mortem {#pre-mortem .detail-only}

::: {.detail-only}

If this synthesis is wrong, the most likely failure modes are:

1. **Underweighting Iranian strategic agency.** M5 (Iran's offensive gambit) is partly inferential. If Iran was actually retaliating defensively rather than coercing strategically, the equilibrium reading is right but the mechanism label is wrong.
2. **The four secondary mechanisms may be redundant rather than independent.** Omnibalancing, 2023 détente, Vision 2030, and Yemen lesson all point toward Sunni Gulf restraint — they may be different symptoms of the same underlying structural condition (Sunni monarchies in a multi-ethnic region with FDI-dependent economies and recent failed-war experience). Treating them as independent risks double-counting.
3. **Over-confidence in the omnibalancing replacement of free-riding.** Gause 2003/4 is in the corpus only via a secondary-source compilation — the original PDF is paywalled. If Gause's actual argument differs from the reconstruction, there is a gap that cannot be closed without acquiring the source.
4. **The DA's framework swap may itself be an over-correction.** Lake's hierarchy predicts client constraints on patron action, but the empirical record (Gulf states accepting US protection across decades; granting basing rights; coordinating on sanctions) shows substantial cooperation that pure clientelism would predict less of. Both free-riding and clientelist constraint may operate.

:::

## How to read the tier badges {.detail-only}

[T1]{.tier .tier-1} **Multi-source verified.** Independent corroboration from at least two distinct sources of different type (e.g., a wire service plus a peer-reviewed analysis).

[T2]{.tier .tier-2} **Single-source named.** Reported by one named source. Not yet independently corroborated.

[T3]{.tier .tier-3} **Inference from evidence.** A reading of empirical evidence under a chosen analytical framework. The factual base is supported but the inferential leap is the analyst's.

[T4]{.tier .tier-4} **Conjecture.** A working hypothesis not yet supported by either named source or strong inference.

:::
